title: Coronary Circulation
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers how the heart supplies its own muscle: the origins, courses, and territories of the coronary arteries, coronary dominance and the papillary muscles, venous drainage through the coronary sinus, and the physiology that sets the coronary bed apart. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, the myocardium extracts about 70% of delivered oxygen at rest, and a rise in demand can be met only by local metabolic vasodilation. The chapter closes with ALCAPA, a congenital lesion that shows these principles failing after birth. Board questions link structure to consequence: they ask which artery was occluded from the infarct leads or complication, or which layer of the wall becomes ischemic first.

sections.title: Origins, courses, and territories of the coronary arteries

blocks.text: Apart from a layer about 0.1 mm thick next to the endocardium, the myocardium depends on two coronary arteries, the first branches of the aorta. They arise from the aortic sinuses, run in surface grooves, and send penetrating branches from epicardium toward endocardium. Each artery supplies the muscle on either side of the groove it occupies, so the grooves predict the territories.

The anterior surface is mostly right ventricle, the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface is mostly left ventricle, and the left surface is the lateral wall. The coronary sulcus (atrioventricular groove) circles the heart between atria and ventricles, the anterior and posterior interventricular grooves mark the septum, and the crux is where the coronary sulcus meets the posterior interventricular groove.
Right coronary artery

The right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right coronary sulcus. It gives a conus branch, the sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery in about 60% of hearts, and the right marginal artery at the acute margin, then reaches the crux, where in most hearts it gives the atrioventricular (AV) nodal artery (about 80%) and turns down the posterior interventricular groove as the posterior descending artery (PDA), which supplies the posterior one-third of the septum and the adjacent inferior wall.
Left main, LAD, and circumflex
The left main coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus and divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex arteries, so its occlusion threatens most of the left ventricle.

The LAD descends in the anterior interventricular groove to the apex. Its septal perforators supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum, which carries the His bundle and both bundle branches, and its diagonal branches supply the anterolateral wall. Because it feeds the largest share of left ventricular muscle, it is the artery most often occluded in infarction, followed by the RCA and then the circumflex. The circumflex follows the left coronary sulcus, supplying the lateral wall through obtuse marginal branches and the left atrium. It usually ends before the crux; when it gives the PDA, the heart is left dominant (section C02).

blocks.text: Why the anatomy matters

Because penetrating branches enter from the epicardium, the subendocardium lies at the far end of every branch (section C04). Territories also predict conduction problems. LAD occlusion can destroy the bundle branches and cause infranodal block, while RCA occlusion causes an inferior infarct that is often accompanied by sinus bradycardia or AV nodal block (CV-7).

Coronary arteries are functional rather than absolute end arteries. Small anastomoses, especially near the apex and in the septum, can enlarge into useful collaterals when a stenosis develops over months, but they cannot protect against a sudden occlusion, which is why an acute thrombus infarcts the territory of the blocked artery.

sections.title: Coronary dominance and the vulnerable posteromedial papillary muscle

blocks.text: Coronary dominance describes which artery gives rise to the PDA, not which artery is larger. The left coronary artery supplies most of the left ventricle in nearly every heart, yet most hearts are right dominant because the RCA gives the PDA. Dominance matters because the PDA supplies the inferior wall, the posterior one-third of the septum, and the posteromedial papillary muscle, and the artery that gives the PDA usually also gives the AV nodal artery.

blocks.title: Patterns of coronary dominance
rows: RCA occlusion causes an inferior infarct, often with AV nodal block; circumflex occlusion stays lateral
Circumflex occlusion causes an inferolateral infarct and can involve the AV node; left main occlusion is even more extensive
Both the RCA and the circumflex reach the posterior interventricular groove
Inferior wall split between two arteries, so either occlusion gives a smaller inferior infarct

blocks.text: Blood supply of the papillary muscles

The papillary muscles pull on the chordae tendineae in systole and keep the mitral leaflets from prolapsing into the left atrium. Their tips lie deep in the cavity, at the end of the coronary branches and within the subendocardium, which makes them highly sensitive to ischemia.

The anterolateral papillary muscle sits where the LAD diagonal and circumflex obtuse marginal territories overlap, so it has a dual supply and rarely ruptures. The posteromedial muscle on the inferior wall usually depends on the PDA alone, so it shares the fate of the PDA whatever its source: the RCA in right-dominant hearts and the circumflex in left-dominant hearts. In commonly quoted series it ruptures about 6 to 12 times as often as the anterolateral muscle, after an inferior infarct.

Rupture occurs most often about 2 to 7 days after infarction. The dead muscle keeps its tensile strength for the first day, but neutrophils then infiltrate and, from about day 3, macrophages remove necrotic myocytes before granulation tissue and collagen can replace them, so systolic traction tears softened tissue (CV-18-C).

blocks.title: From inferior infarct to papillary muscle rupture
steps: Thrombus occludes the artery giving the PDA
Posteromedial papillary muscle loses its only supply
Coagulative necrosis of the papillary muscle
Neutrophils, then macrophages, soften it over days 2 to 7
Systolic traction tears the muscle or one head
Chordae lose their anchor; mitral leaflets flail
Acute severe mitral regurgitation
blocks.caption: The occluded artery depends on dominance, but the chain is the same: single supply, necrosis, enzymatic softening, rupture.

blocks.text: Manifestations explained by mechanism

Sudden mitral incompetence ejects much of each stroke volume into a normal-sized, relatively stiff left atrium. Left atrial pressure rises steeply and causes abrupt pulmonary edema, while forward stroke volume falls, causing hypotension and possibly cardiogenic shock. The murmur may be short and soft because the gradient across the valve collapses before systole ends. Post-infarct septal rupture also causes sudden decompensation with a new systolic murmur, but it produces an oxygen saturation step-up from right atrium to right ventricle. Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction without rupture is more common and causes milder regurgitation.

blocks.predict: Why does an occluded LAD, which causes the largest infarcts, rarely cause papillary muscle rupture?
blocks.explain: The anterolateral papillary muscle in the LAD region also receives circumflex branches, so losing the LAD alone leaves it perfused. The posteromedial muscle lies outside the LAD territory in most hearts. Rupture requires a muscle that has lost its only supply.

sections.title: Cardiac venous drainage and the coronary sinus

blocks.text: Coronary veins follow the arteries back to the coronary sulcus, and most converge on the coronary sinus. About 75% of total coronary flow returns through the sinus, mainly the venous blood of the left ventricle, while most right ventricular venous blood returns through the anterior cardiac veins.
The coronary sinus

The coronary sinus is a wide, thin-walled channel in the posterior coronary sulcus between the left atrium and left ventricle. It opens into the right atrium between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid orifice, partly guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus, and its ostium forms one border of the triangle that locates the AV node (CV-7).

The sinus begins where the great cardiac vein meets the oblique vein of the left atrium, a remnant of the embryonic left superior vena cava, and it develops from the left horn of the sinus venosus. A persistent left superior vena cava therefore drains into a dilated coronary sinus, usually harmlessly, because the blood still reaches the right atrium.
Tributaries and veins that bypass the sinus

Each named vein shadows an artery: the great cardiac vein runs with the LAD and then the circumflex, the middle cardiac vein with the PDA, and the small cardiac vein with the right marginal artery. Two groups bypass the sinus. The anterior cardiac veins open directly into the right atrium, and the smallest cardiac veins (venae cordis minimae) drain capillary beds straight into the chambers, mostly the atria, although some open into the left ventricle.

blocks.text: Physiological consequences

Because the myocardium extracts about 70% of delivered oxygen (section C04), coronary sinus blood is only about 25% to 30% saturated, among the most deoxygenated blood in the body at rest, compared with about 75% in mixed venous blood. Coronary sinus blood therefore reflects left ventricular oxygen extraction and lactate release.

Smallest cardiac veins that open into the left heart, together with bronchial venous blood draining into the pulmonary veins, form the normal physiological shunt of about 2% of cardiac output. This is one reason arterial PO2 is slightly below alveolar PO2 and the normal alveolar to arterial PO2 difference is not zero.

sections.title: Diastolic perfusion, high oxygen extraction, and subendocardial vulnerability

blocks.text: Coronary flow is about 225 mL/min at rest, about 4% to 5% of cardiac output, for an organ about 0.5% of body weight.
Diastolic perfusion of the left ventricle

In systole, intramyocardial pressure in the inner wall rises to about cavity pressure and squeezes the vessels shut, so flow falls sharply (and can briefly reverse) as systole begins and surges in early diastole when compression is released. About 70% to 80% of left ventricular flow occurs in diastole. The right ventricle, at about 25 mmHg systolic, is perfused throughout the cycle unless pulmonary hypertension raises its pressure toward systemic levels.

Left ventricular coronary perfusion pressure is about aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), because diastolic cavity pressure acts as the back pressure on the inner vessels. Hypotension and aortic regurgitation lower the first term, and heart failure and a stiff hypertrophied ventricle raise the second.
High oxygen extraction

Arterial blood carries about 20 mL O2/dL and coronary sinus blood about 5 to 6 mL/dL, so the myocardium extracts about 70% to 75% at rest (about 25% for the whole body). Myocytes contract continuously and make almost all their ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, with mitochondria filling about one-third of cell volume, small creatine phosphate stores, and little anaerobic capacity. About one capillary per myocyte and cytoplasmic myoglobin ease diffusion, so the heart extracts most of the oxygen at rest and has little left to recruit (section C05).
Subendocardial vulnerability

The subendocardium lies at the end of the penetrating branches, receives almost no systolic flow, faces LVEDP in diastole, and has the highest wall stress and oxygen demand. Lower resting arteriolar tone normally gives it slightly more flow per gram than the subepicardium, but this spends part of its vasodilator reserve at rest, so it runs out first when perfusion pressure falls, diastole shortens, or demand rises.

By the law of Laplace, wall stress is proportional to cavity pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, so high afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) and dilation (heart failure) raise oxygen demand. Hypertrophy lowers stress, but capillaries lag behind muscle growth and the stiff wall raises LVEDP.

blocks.title: How tachycardia produces subendocardial ischemia
steps: Heart rate rises (exercise, fever, anemia, arrhythmia)
Diastole shortens far more than systole
Diastolic perfusion time per minute falls
Each extra beat raises oxygen demand
Subendocardium exhausts its vasodilator reserve
Inner wall ischemia: angina and ST depression
blocks.caption: Tachycardia lowers supply and raises demand at the same time.

blocks.title: Diastolic time per minute at two heart rates
blocks.text: At 70 bpm a cycle lasts about 0.86 s. With systole about 0.30 s, diastole is about 0.56 s, or about 39 s per minute. At 150 bpm a cycle lasts 0.40 s, and systole shortens only to about 0.22 s, leaving about 0.18 s, or about 27 s of diastole per minute. Demand has risen, yet left ventricular perfusion time has fallen by about 30%. If a stenosis already limits arteriolar dilation, flow cannot compensate and the subendocardium becomes ischemic first, which is why exercise in coronary stenosis produces ST depression.

Ischemia can therefore occur with normal coronary arteries. Aortic stenosis raises systolic pressure, muscle mass, and LVEDP, and aortic regurgitation lowers aortic diastolic pressure and dilates the ventricle. In severe anemia or hypoxemia, extraction is already near its limit, so lower arterial oxygen content cuts delivery directly.

blocks.predict: A patient with severe aortic regurgitation has a blood pressure of 150/40 mmHg and an LVEDP of 25 mmHg. Estimate the coronary perfusion pressure and predict which layer of the left ventricle is most at risk.
blocks.explain: About 40 minus 25, or 15 mmHg, far below the normal of about 70 mmHg (80 minus 8). Low diastolic perfusion pressure plus the high wall stress of a dilated ventricle threaten the subendocardium first.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraphs on perfusion pressure and the subendocardium.

sections.title: Local metabolic control of coronary flow

blocks.text: Because extraction is nearly maximal at rest, the heart meets higher demand by raising flow in proportion to oxygen consumption. Myocyte metabolites dilate the arterioles that feed them, overriding most neural influences.

By the Fick principle, myocardial oxygen consumption equals coronary flow times the arteriovenous oxygen content difference. Skeletal muscle can widen that difference in exercise, but the myocardium already extracts about 70% to 75% at rest and can reach only about 80% to 90%, so flow is the only term left to change.

blocks.title: Using the Fick principle to show why the heart must raise flow
blocks.text: Take resting flow as 2.25 dL/min, arterial O2 content 20 mL/dL, and coronary venous content 6 mL/dL. The arteriovenous difference is 14 mL/dL, so consumption is about 32 mL O2/min and extraction is 70%. Now double demand to about 63 mL/min. Raising extraction to its maximum of about 85% (17 mL/dL) at fixed flow gives only about 38 mL/min. Keeping extraction near 70% requires a flow of 63 divided by 14, about 4.5 dL/min, double the resting value. Only higher flow meets the demand, so any lesion that limits the rise in flow causes ischemia under stress.
Adenosine and other metabolic vasodilators

When supply falls short, ATP breakdown outpaces regeneration and AMP accumulates. The enzyme 5 prime nucleotidase converts AMP to adenosine, which diffuses to arteriolar smooth muscle and binds A2A receptors. Gs raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A (PKA), which opens K+ channels, including ATP-sensitive (KATP) channels. Hyperpolarization closes L-type Ca2+ channels, cytosolic Ca2+ falls, myosin light chain kinase activity drops, and the arteriole relaxes.

blocks.title: Adenosine-mediated coronary vasodilation
steps: Myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply
ATP breakdown outpaces regeneration; AMP accumulates
5 prime nucleotidase converts AMP to adenosine
Adenosine binds arteriolar A2A receptors (Gs, cAMP, PKA)
K+ channels open; hyperpolarization reduces L-type Ca2+ entry
Arteriolar smooth muscle relaxes; resistance falls
Flow rises until supply matches demand
blocks.caption: A negative feedback loop: adenosine rises with the oxygen deficit and is cleared within seconds by cellular uptake and adenosine deaminase.

blocks.text: Blocking adenosine receptors blunts but does not abolish the rise in flow, so other mediators act in parallel: low PO2 and ATP opening KATP channels directly, CO2, H+, and lactate, K+ released by repeated depolarization, and endothelial nitric oxide released by shear stress. Sympathetic alpha-1 constriction is mild, while beta-1 stimulation raises cardiac work and metabolite release, so sympathetic activation raises coronary flow overall.
Autoregulation, flow reserve, and steal

The same local mechanisms autoregulate flow, holding it nearly constant over a perfusion pressure range of about 60 to 140 mmHg, so at rest the arterioles keep spare dilating capacity. This coronary flow reserve, maximal flow divided by resting flow, is normally about 3 to 5. A fixed epicardial stenosis consumes the reserve as downstream arterioles dilate to offset it. Maximal flow starts to fall at about 50% diameter narrowing, while resting flow is preserved until about 80% or more. This is the mechanism of stable angina: flow is adequate at rest, but with exertion the arterioles are already dilated and the subendocardium becomes ischemic (CV-18-C).

Coronary steal follows from the same physiology. A vasodilator such as adenosine, or dipyridamole, which blocks cellular adenosine uptake, dilates normal beds while the bed beyond a stenosis is already maximally dilated. Flow shifts toward normal myocardium and can fall in the ischemic bed, the basis of pharmacologic stress perfusion imaging.

blocks.predict: A patient has a 75% diameter stenosis of the LAD. Predict coronary flow in that territory at rest and during exercise, and explain why the patient feels well while sitting.
blocks.explain: At rest, downstream arterioles dilate enough to offset the stenosis, so flow is normal. Because part of the reserve is already spent at rest, exercise exhausts the rest, maximal flow falls short of demand, and the subendocardium becomes ischemic first.

sections.title: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery

blocks.text: In anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA), the left main coronary artery arises from the pulmonary trunk while the RCA arises normally from the aorta. It is rare but an important cause of myocardial infarction in infancy.
Why the lesion is tolerated before birth and fails after

Before birth, high pulmonary vascular resistance and the ductus arteriosus keep pulmonary artery pressure about equal to aortic pressure, so the anomalous artery fills antegrade at systemic pressure. Fetal pulmonary artery blood is only modestly less saturated than ascending aortic blood, and the fetal myocardium is adapted to low oxygen tension, so the heart develops normally.

After birth, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, the ductus closes, and pulmonary artery pressure falls over days to weeks toward about 25/10 mmHg. The left coronary artery now carries low-pressure blood that is only about 70% to 75% saturated, which cannot supply a left ventricle that is perfused mainly in diastole against LVEDP and extracts about 70% of its oxygen. Collaterals from the RCA, still at aortic pressure, fill the left coronary branches, but because the pulmonary trunk is the lowest-pressure outlet, blood flows backward up the left coronary artery into it. The left coronary artery becomes a drain, a form of coronary steal, and the left ventricle stays ischemic despite growing collateral flow.

blocks.title: From normal birth transition to infant myocardial ischemia
steps: Before birth, pulmonary artery pressure equals aortic pressure; antegrade filling
After birth, pulmonary resistance falls and the ductus closes
Left coronary artery receives low-pressure, desaturated blood
RCA collaterals fill the left coronary branches
Flow reverses into the low-pressure pulmonary trunk (steal)
Anterolateral ischemia and infarction, often at 2 to 3 months
blocks.caption: The lesion becomes symptomatic as the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary pressure removes the only pressure source the left coronary artery had.

blocks.text: Manifestations explained by mechanism

Symptoms usually begin around 2 to 3 months, once pulmonary pressure has reached its low postnatal level, and not in the first days, when it is still high. Feeding is an infant's main exertion, so ischemia appears with feeds or crying as pallor, sweating, irritability, and breathlessness, described as infant angina. The dilating, poorly contracting ventricle then causes heart failure with tachypnea, poor weight gain, and cardiomegaly. The ECG shows an anterolateral infarct pattern, with abnormal Q waves and ST and T changes in I, aVL, V5, and V6, which is almost unheard of in a normal infant. Anterolateral papillary muscle ischemia and annular dilation cause mitral regurgitation.

blocks.title: Self-reinforcing ischemia in ALCAPA
steps: Low-pressure flow and steal leave the left ventricle ischemic
Ischemic ventricle contracts poorly and dilates
Larger radius raises wall stress and oxygen demand
Papillary ischemia and annular dilation cause mitral regurgitation
LVEDP rises and perfusion pressure falls further
Ischemia deepens and drives further dilation
blocks.caption: Each consequence of ischemia either raises demand or lowers supply, so the infant left ventricle can deteriorate quickly.

blocks.text: Variability and distinctions

Most infants have limited collaterals and develop severe ischemia and heart failure in the first year, with high mortality if the lesion is not recognized. A minority develop extensive RCA collaterals and survive into childhood or adulthood with a dilated RCA, a continuous murmur, mitral regurgitation, exercise-induced ischemia, or sudden arrhythmic death. In these patients pulmonary artery saturation may be slightly higher than right ventricular saturation because of the small left-to-right shunt from the coronary system.

A regional infarct in the left coronary territory in an infant whose symptoms began after the first weeks distinguishes ALCAPA from dilated cardiomyopathy and myocarditis. A coexisting lesion that keeps pulmonary pressure high, such as a large ventricular septal defect, can delay or mask the ischemia, because the critical variable is pulmonary artery pressure relative to the pressure needed to perfuse the left ventricle, not the anomalous origin itself.

integration.text: Anatomy sets the territories: each coronary artery supplies the muscle beside its groove, the veins return along the same grooves, and the artery that reaches the crux decides which occlusion threatens the inferior wall, the AV node, and the posteromedial papillary muscle. Embryology explains the variants, from a persistent left superior vena cava draining into the coronary sinus to ALCAPA. Physiology and biochemistry explain the behavior of the bed: continuous oxidative metabolism forces near-maximal extraction at rest, adenosine and other metabolites match flow to demand, and systolic compression confines left ventricular perfusion to diastole, so heart rate, aortic diastolic pressure, LVEDP, and wall stress decide whether supply meets demand.

Pathology follows from these principles. A stenosis consumes flow reserve and causes exertional angina, an acute thrombus infarcts a territory and produces complications predicted by the structures in it, and aortic valve disease, hypertrophy, anemia, and sustained tachycardia can cause subendocardial ischemia without coronary disease. Territories are predictions to be confirmed by ECG or imaging, since dominance, nodal artery origin, and collateral development vary between individuals.

summary: The RCA runs in the right coronary sulcus and supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, the SA node in about 60% and the AV node in about 80% of hearts.
The left main divides into the LAD (anterior wall, apex, anterior two-thirds of the septum with the bundle branches) and the circumflex (lateral wall and left atrium).
Dominance is defined only by which artery gives the PDA; most hearts are right dominant, so an inferior infarct usually implicates the RCA.
The posteromedial papillary muscle depends on the PDA alone and ruptures about 2 to 7 days after an inferior infarct, causing acute severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema.

The great, middle, and small cardiac veins follow the LAD and circumflex, the PDA, and the right marginal artery into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium; anterior and smallest cardiac veins bypass it.
Systolic compression confines most left ventricular flow to diastole, and coronary perfusion pressure is about aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP.
The myocardium extracts about 70% to 75% of arterial oxygen at rest, so by the Fick principle a rise in demand must be met by a rise in flow.
Adenosine from ATP breakdown acts on A2A receptors (Gs, cAMP, K+ channel opening) to dilate arterioles, with low PO2, CO2, H+, K+, and nitric oxide contributing.
The subendocardium becomes ischemic first because of systolic compression, exposure to LVEDP, the highest wall stress, and the least remaining vasodilator reserve; tachycardia worsens all of these.

In ALCAPA, the postnatal fall in pulmonary pressure leaves the left coronary artery with low-pressure, desaturated blood, and RCA collateral flow drains into the pulmonary trunk, causing anterolateral infarction in early infancy.

verify: Frequencies of right dominance (quoted from about 67% to 85%), left dominance, and codominance differ between anatomical and angiographic series; confirm the figures NABNE expects.
SA nodal artery origin (about 60% RCA, 40% circumflex) and AV nodal artery origin (about 80% RCA) vary among sources; values here match those used in CV-7.
The fraction of left ventricular flow that occurs in diastole is quoted in a range (often about 70% to 80%); the exact figure varies between sources.
The ratio of posteromedial to anterolateral papillary muscle rupture (about 6 to 12 times) is quoted from clinical series and varies; confirm whether a ratio is tested.
The rupture window after infarction is given here as about 2 to 7 days; Robbins and other sources give slightly different ranges (for example 3 to 7 days).

Coronary sinus oxygen saturation (about 25% to 30%), maximal myocardial extraction (about 80% to 90%), coronary flow reserve (about 3 to 5), and the autoregulatory range (about 60 to 140 mmHg) are approximate consensus values that differ slightly between Guyton and Hall and Boron and Boulpaep.
Stenosis thresholds (maximal flow falling at about 50% diameter narrowing, resting flow falling at about 80% or more) come from classic experimental work and are approximations.

The usual age at presentation of ALCAPA (often about 2 to 3 months) and the statement that most untreated infants die in the first year come from pediatric cardiology series; confirm against current references and whether NABNE expects the eponym Bland-White-Garland syndrome.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I uses the term venae cordis minimae, Thebesian veins, or smallest cardiac veins, and whether the valve of the coronary sinus is expected by name.
